item.title: Artspace Guåhan to open ‘You Are Here’ exhibition
item.description: Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning. The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.
item.content:encoded:
Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning.

The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.

The exhibition centers on the question, “What does HERE mean to YOU?” and invites visitors to consider their own connections to place and belonging through the artwork on display.

Artspace Guåhan will bring together artists with different perspectives and ask visitors to consider what being “ here ” means to them. Deane Jessee-Jones, secretary of the board of directors, says the exhibition supports local artists of varying ages.

She said, “We do not collect any commission… all of the profits go directly to the artist.”

Artspace Guåhan is a Guam-based nonprofit that works to make art accessible and provide opportunities for local artists to exhibit and connect with the community.

The opening runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. and will include an opportunity to meet the artists.

The exhibition will remain on display through Dec. 3.

You Are Here is free and open to the public.

item.title: U.S. Supreme Court hears arguments in Andersen open detonation case
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base. The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base.

The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.

In May 2021, the Air Force applied for a three-year renewal of its hazardous waste facility permit with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency. In court filings, Prutehi Guåhan stated that the Air Force failed to conduct an environmental assessment of its actions as required by the National Environmental Policy Act.

The case was dismissed in the District Court of Guam, but the 9 th Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Prutehi Guåhan and reinstated the case.

The Supreme Court is considering whether the Air Force’s request to renew its permit would be a “final agency action” that can be reviewed by the courts. Justices are also considering whether federal agencies must comply with NEPA requirements before seeking to renew environmental permits.

During oral arguments before the court, Department of Justice attorney Sopan Joshi argued that filing a permit application is not a final agency action.

“It’s a request to someone else to take action,” he said. “Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee, asked Joshi when the Air Force’s decision to operate the detonation pit would be considered final.

“So are you saying that there’s no point at which the Air Force’s decision can be challenged?” he asked. “The Air Force’s action is never final and, therefore, never reviewable?”

“The application is never going to become final agency action,” Joshi said. “And there is no cause of action under NEPA itself. Congress didn't provide one. So any review would have to go through the [Administrative Procedure Act], and I don't think the APA provides a cause of action for this application at any point in time.”

Earthjustice attorney Caroline Flynn, representing Prutehi Guåhan, said the Air Force’s final action is clear.

“We know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.”

The justices will consider the arguments, and a ruling will likely take several months.

item.title: ‘Struggling to keep this government going’: Apatang warns of furloughs, rising austerity after signing strained CNMI budget
item.description: The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues. Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.
item.content:encoded:
The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues.

Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.

Apatang said he vetoed several provisions he deemed unconstitutional or financially impossible, including a mandate requiring the administration to “front‑load” $16 million to the Public School System. He said the CNMI cannot afford the upfront payment and must instead fund PSS monthly. The Senate’s final budget version allocates $25 million for PSS—down from the $32 million proposed by both the governor and the House.

“It breaks my heart to reduce PSS funding,” Apatang said, adding that a three‑day school week would be unacceptable but may be unavoidable unless the PSS board finds operational efficiencies.

The governor said the administration is “scraping the bottom of the barrel,” warning that furloughs—estimated at up to 400 employees—may be necessary once Civil Service Commission regulations are finalized. He also confirmed retirees will lose their 25% government contribution after Oct. 15, though he is searching for funds to soften the impact.

Apatang defended his administration against criticism over the CNMI’s fiscal collapse, saying he inherited years of unresolved audit findings and depleted federal relief funds.

“I didn’t spend all this money,” he said. “We’re struggling to keep this government going.”

He urged agencies to tighten operations, reduce expenses, and avoid unnecessary vehicle use. He also asked Commonwealth Public Utilities Corp. to reconsider CUC’s proposed rate increase, calling it “a drastic burden” residents cannot afford.

On tourism and economic recovery, Apatang said federal immigration and travel policies continue to hinder the CNMI’s ability to rebuild air service and visitor arrivals. He said he has repeatedly asked federal officials to visit the Commonwealth and understand its strategic importance.

With three months left in his term, Apatang said the next administration will face a difficult road.

“Good luck,” he said. “I’ll pray for you. It’s going to be a tough one.”

item.title: Discursive Verses: Vic Mensa and the rise of a rap manosphere counterculture

item.content:encoded:
In the middle of Vic Mensa's sit-down with Rapsody on the third episode of The Vic Mensa Show, the rapper-turned-podcaster recalled "one of the most quintessential moments in Black thought." He was paying reverence to a 1971 conversation between poet Nikki Giovanni and writer James Baldwin. Though that dialogue happened more than 50 years ago, the moment has become an ever-present meme in recent years for embodying the gender gap that can make Black love and Black survival feel like contradictory pursuits.

While ruminating over that classic exchange, Rapsody and Mensa stumble onto a new question: "Where do Black men go to cry?" To which Mensa admits he finds refuge alone in the shower. "You've been convinced that vulnerability is weak," he says. "And you grow and you realize that it was a damn lie — that having vulnerability is far stronger than having some false machismo masculinity."

In that moment, Rapsody casually rises and reaches over to wipe the tears streaming down Mensa's face. "I'm glad that you could cry my brother," she responds. And with that, I had to hit pause just to register what happened. It's got to be the most tender and vulnerable exchange on a podcast I've ever witnessed.

For at least a decade now, podcasts have felt like rap's final frontier. Or an early retirement home for rappers with no pension parlaying their onstage talents into sideshow hosts. The medium launched by the original hip-hop podcast Juan Ep and its contemporary The Combat Jack Show gave way to a generation that cooked down the original formula, like crack, and distilled it to its lowest common denominator. Longform interviews and deep liner notes mostly gave way to trash talk, street gossip and celebrity-driven opinions dredged from our broader cultural obsession with fame, power and success.

In a space currently overrun by chatty patties, as Dame Dash famously declared, the freshest podders on hot mics are offering a counterweight to rap's reigning manosphere of podcast bros. I like to think of them as the podcast bruhs — an ideological alternative to the moderately conservative mainstream. Like the difference between rage-baiting and righteously raging against the machine. If one end is ruled by two of the highest-paid podcasters ranked by Forbes, Joe Budden and Charlamagne tha God, the other side is propped up by the likes of everyman Deante Kyle, a relative newcomer who only quit his truck driving gig a year ago to host the Grits & Eggs Podcast full-time.

Still, content is big business. Even in a beleaguered industry, Charlemagne tha God secured a $200 million bag. His Black Effect joint partnership with iHeart Podcasts now counts nearly 50 titles among a targeted roster it rolls out with the pace of a deep-pocketed major label in the '90s. Podcasting has also become an extension of the art form. Or performance art, per se. When Jadakiss throws a flag on his co-host Fat Joe's flagrant fouls, we're all in on the gag. What cats like Mensa, Deante Kyle, and even scholar Marc Lamont Hill are delivering is a type of performance, too. (Detractors might even call them "performative.") But their roles are steeped in a Black liberation politic that is equal parts sensitive, radical and intersectional. Even if they're just a blip on the dial of toxic, misogynistic, materialistic content, they're a blip worth watching.

The Rapsody episode wasn't Mensa's first intimate moment with a guest. The first one happened when he confided through tears to his friend Chance the Rapper how much it hurt him — and his pockets — when Chance decided against inviting Vic on tour years ago. Chance didn't try to wipe away those tears like Rapsody, but he did take a beat to empathize with Vic and apologize.

Toxicity loves company, and corporations love cashing in on the contagion with zero regard for its harmful effects. Mostly what these pods provide is a critical voice in a field where anything other than mindless praise is viewed as knocking the hustle.

Like a Five Percenter with the delivery of a Southern preacher, Kyle's community-minded commentary is uncut and unforgiving. Black celebrities get zero passes. When Jay-Z's boycott-busting, exclusive vinyl deal with Target backfired this summer, Kyle pulled no punches. "I don't know too much about Jay-Z personally," he said. "I will tell you this. The n**** hates a protest." Even LeBron's recent $15 million Polymarket deal, which will keep him afloat more than his NBA paycheck this year, came under Kyle's crosshairs. "Essentially, what LeBron James does is he helps usher in the newest generation of junkies," he said on an episode titled "Polymarket Pimps."

Mensa's podcast is a spinoff of the heavily-parodied, viral "Orange Tree" shorts that found him kicking anti-capitalist ballistics in a tank-top surrounded by citrus. His lineup of guests highlight a cross-section of Black culture from rap-adjacent to queer-friendly, including like-minded podcaster Van Lathan and singer Durand Bernarr. Mensa has also spoken about the challenge of securing funding for his show while avoiding gambling's sweeping marketing push. Meanwhile, Joe Budden shows no shame in pitching his biggest sponsor, the prediction market site Prize Picks, during paid advertorials every episode.

But Budden clearly senses a shift, too. In 2024, he made the strategic move to add Hill to his show's panel of homies and industry cronies. Whenever the CUNY professor rushes to some notable woman's defense, his couch mates cringe so much that it's become a predictable JBP bit. Clearly, he challenges the pod — and its millions of monthly listeners and viewers — with his feminist, abolitionist views. While there's no metric to measure Hill's positive impact, the move itself suggests how much Budden recognizes that his weekly conversations — which he clearly sees as a microcosm of the culture — are in desperate need of more intersectional thought.

In an era of anti-wokeness, it's refreshing to find a few bruhs who refuse to sleepwalk.

These three figures alone are not the complete list, nor are they necessarily indicative of a trend. However, they make up a vanguard (along with leftist streamers and YouTube essayists) that seems to be rising up in meaningful corners of the Internet to help reclaim some space for the Black radical tradition. The younger audiences they serve are down to engage in the kind of dialogue and ideas that grounded forebears like Baldwin and Giovanni. Only once we start to have those conversations more freely and openly can we decolonize our minds, too.

item.title: Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.
item.description: My brother took his own life on May 10, 2010. Rarely a day goes by that I don't think of him. But just because I thought about him, it didn't mean I could talk about him. For a long time, I couldn't. Sometimes when the subject of suicide came up, I would want to — or literally have to — leave wherever I was. Not helpful if you're in the news business.
item.content:encoded:
My brother took his own life on May 10, 2010. Rarely a day goes by that I don't think of him. But just because I thought about him, it didn't mean I could talk about him. For a long time, I couldn't.

Sometimes when the subject of suicide came up, I would want to — or literally have to — leave wherever I was. Not helpful if you're in the news business.

I've come to realize that I have to talk about it. We have to talk about it.

Why do we have to? Because our silence is not protecting us.

Suicide is a public health crisis for the country — but that crisis is becoming acute in the Black community. Black suicide rates are climbing, increasing more than 50% over about the past 10 years according to CDC data. And the suicide rates among Black youth are increasing particularly dramatically. The rate of Black youth suicides by firearms exceeded that of white youth in 2022.

At a time when government-sponsored public health initiatives are retreating from issues that impact different communities differently, we're going there with care, sensitivity and honesty.

I hosted an NPR's Morning Edition live event called Going There: A Matter of Life and Death. It brought together a panel of clinicians, lawmakers and people who have lived with this pain to talk about this epidemic, in front of a live audience who have also experienced it. Speakers include CEO emerita of BET Debra Lee, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-NJ, psychiatrist Dr. Paul Nestadt, retired NFL champion Vernon Davis, WWE superstar Ettore "Big E" Ewen and Rev. Johnny Parker, who is both a pastor and a counselor.

It was an attempt to try to find out why this crisis is happening, how it is affecting us, and most importantly, what we can do about it.

During the conversation, Super Bowl-winning tight end Vernon Davis shared his struggles with panic attacks and depression.

"I would have these episodes in the game," Davis said, "I would go sit on a bench and breathe hard. I just felt like, for a split second, that I didn't want to be here. I had nothing to live for. It happened so fast, and it was just so sudden."

Davis now says that focusing on his mental health is a daily priority. And, after Davis lost both his brother and sister in quick succession, he started speaking more openly about his experiences with mental health.

"There's people out there who are going through the same thing that I went through," he explained, "they just need to hear that there's someone else out there that is going through the same thing."

Dr. Paul Nestadt is a psychiatrist, medical director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention, and a national authority on suicide. He notes that white people still account for the majority of suicide deaths, and the suicide rate has decreased slightly among white Americans. Meanwhile, the rate has gone up among Black Americans. Access to guns accounts for at least part of that increase.

"When that trend in young Black people, especially young Black males, started to go up was also a time when we saw a dramatic increase in firearm ownership in the Black community. That was in 2020, in the context of the pandemic, the murder of George Floyd, and a variety of other things," Nestadt said.

As a result, 2025 survey data shows the lowest rate of self-reported suicide attempts among young Black people in America in years. But, Nestadt said, "the death rate has gone higher than it's ever been. And that just comes down to the fact that when an attempt is made, now with so many more guns in the house, that attempt is fatal."

Nestadt emphasized that it is crucial to correct several prevailing myths about suicide: chiefly that only people with long-term mental illnesses are vulnerable and that mentioning that you are concerned that someone might take their own life plants the idea. Neither is true. He says suicide is often an impulsive act, and interrupting that thought can work.

Every panelist brought similar words of wisdom. Among the most important advice:

There's a lot we can do to support each other and take care of ourselves.

And if you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can reach someone 24 hours a day, just to talk or to help get access to care.

item.title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego
item.description: The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically res
item.content:encoded:
The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

Hegseth told the crew that President Donald Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."

The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.

The Navy initially downplayed any problems, and Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."

The carrier had left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.

Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

item.title: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
item.description: NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations. Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during h
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations.

Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.

The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power.

"This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."

Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.

A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.

The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.

They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.

Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.

Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.

Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.

While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.

Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.

Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.

In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito."

"It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations."

Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.

They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture.

Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an "extreme" flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.

U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores' request. He noted, among other things, that she's unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.

He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she's already on medication for that.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
